utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic. We are continuing with your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is ready, his name is Dario Radic and I suggest that we call this witness and my colleague Krgovic will be present at this examination-in-chief. I will take this opportunity, Your Honours, just to tell you something which may not be for the transcript but we, as Defence counsel, would like to point out or rather commend a group of people who were helping us with the depositions who -- before we mainly had objections to the work of some services; however, the witness protection service has been very helpful in preparing these depositions and they were done very well and under extremely difficult weather conditions and their drivers also did a good job so on behalf of all our colleagues we would like to inform the Chamber, because thanks to them, these depositions have been made in the best possible way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure the Trial Chamber would like to add its thanks to the Defence counsel and the other parties as well for the good work that they did to support the work of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. If I may, we have some problems with our transcript on laptop computer, so if someone from the technical unit can come in the meantime, I would appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. That will be attended to. Can the witness please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Dario Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: On the 6th of October, in 1974.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, where are your parents from?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My father was born in Bosanski Samac and my mother was from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises for not getting the name of the place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters didn't get the name of the place for the birth of the mother, I think, one of the particulars. If you look at the transcript, it's not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, can you tell us where your parents were born?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My father was born in Samac and mother in Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: In Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, let me just ask you, after you heard my question, can you please make a pause a few seconds before you start your answer so that the interpreters can do their job properly and avoid overlapping because the two of us speak the same language and it is really necessary that everything that we talk about is being translated so please wait for a couple of seconds after I've finished my question and then start your answer. Mr. Radic, your parents, what is their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My parents are Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, are you married?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what education you have?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I completed mechanical secondary school for metal lathe worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, are you employed?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I work for the football club Borac from Samac. I work as a waiter at the cafe there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did you complete military service?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year did you start your military service and when did you complete it?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I started my military service on the 4th of May, 1993 and I returned from the army on the 6th of May, 1993. I completed my military service in my units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, did you have any rank in the army?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krgovic, just for the sake of clarity, the Witness' answer on page 4, lines 11 and 12 don't strike me as making sense in terms of the dates. He started -- he says, "I started my military service on 4th of May, 1993 and I returned from the army on the 6th of May, 1993," two days. Maybe we could get that rectified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us, Mr. Radic, when did you leave the army?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I returned from the army in late 1994 so my military service lasted about two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned these dates, 4th and 6th of May, 1993, can you explain to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: From the 4th of May -- on the 4th of May, I was sent to Bijeljina to serve in the army. Then, they accepted me there, gave me an assignment, and on the 4th and the 5th, we had an introductory or basic training, turn to the left, turn to the right, et cetera, and then in the evening of the 5th of May, a commander, a squad commander called me and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, that isn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the 5th of May, you returned to Bosanski Samac and you continued there. Mr. Radic, tell us where do you live in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Nikola Pasicic Street number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With whom did you used to live before the war, before the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I lived with my father and mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any other relatives -- in Bosanski Samac before April 1992, did you have any other relatives?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I have three aunts and I had an uncle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They all used to live in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, tell me, are you a member of any party? Repeated question: Were you a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about your father?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My father was, before the war, in the communist party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When multiparty elections were held and when national-based parties were formed, did your father join any of those new parties?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Neither did I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in the period before the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, had you noticed anything unusual in Bosanski Samac, were there any changes as compared to your life before that time?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The situation was tense and on the day, there were separations, Serbs on the one side, Muslims on the other, and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any cooling of relations between people of different ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: At the time, before that particular day came, I used to socialise with the Serbs and the Muslims and Croats. That was before this day came, we all spent time together and maintained good relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, do you know, did the people immediately before the 16th and 17th of April, did they flee Samac, did they put their families away, was there any mention of any pending attack?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I didn't believe that myself, but there were families who went to Serbia or to Croatia if they had any place to take their families to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, can you tell us, where were you on the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: On that night between the 16th and the 17th, or rather in the evening, I was in a cafe with a couple of friends, we had a few drinks, and a friend of mine, Jasmin Peles, we set off to have some good time after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, what ethnicity is Mr. Jasmin Peles?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you headed?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I headed to the memorial centre where there was a night club there and he went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That was about 2.00 or half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean a.m.?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, in the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, which route you had to take in order to reach the memorial centre?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: We had to go down the main street and on that street, there was a SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the police building?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When we set off. We didn't notice anything, but when we passed some 50 metres or came at some 50 metres from the SUP building, there were no lights on and I felt that something was wrong. Then, with a friend of mine, I proceeded but after some 10 metres, special policemen burst out in camouflage uniforms with their caps on their heads and with their faces painted. They told us to raise our hands in the air. They asked us if we were armed. We didn't have any weapons. Whatever we had in our pockets, a certain amount of money, it was taken away from us, and then they took us inside the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, which accent did those people speak in?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They spoke in the Serbian accent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they stopped you, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ask you about your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When we entered the SUP building, they asked me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your answer?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I told them that I was a Croat and my friend said that he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next, were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They arrested us and took us -- there were two cells in the SUP and they locked us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, where were those cells, on the ground floor or on the upper floor?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The cells were on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, when you were brought in, were there any other individuals in the cells?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: There were some five or six policemen who were there on duty in their uniforms and other people who went to work or something like that, they were all locked up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were all locked?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, during that time, those days, were you questioned or interrogated by anyone?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: On the Friday, around 1.00 or 2.00 p.m., was called to come to the upper floor in the SUP for -- to be questioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say Friday?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, I was detained on the night between Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would be the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, where were you taken to the upper floor, to an office?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, to an office. I was called to come to an office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who questioned you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I was questioned by the Serbs, these special policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Serbs, you mean people from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, special policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those were not the Serbs from Samac, the people who questioned you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, those were not people were Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the questioning last?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I was questioned between 15 and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They asked me what my ethnicity is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you answer?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That I am a Croat. They asked me if I had weapons. I said that I didn't. If I was in any party, I responded that I wasn't. And then they asked me about my father, whether he was in any party, and if he had weapons. He didn't have any weapons either, nor was he a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did they beat you during that interrogation?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When I was interrogated, I wasn't beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell us where did they return you after the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: After the interrogation, they took me back to the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time did you spend at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I spent the time there from Thursday and Friday, three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were there, did you see anybody beating the detainees?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the SUP, in this cell on the ground floor, did anybody come in to beat you or the other inmates?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I was involved with my own misfortune that night, Friday night, a member of the special forces came in, he -- his nickname was Lugar, he took me out into the corridor and hit me on my back with a baton six or seven times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, during the time that you were at the SUP, did you receive any food?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: We didn't receive any food, but some of those members of the special forces would hide tins of food and chocolate and bread for us so that those who were the most dangerous amongst them wouldn't see that we were eating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to go to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to go, but they escorted us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, while you were at the SUP, were you taken out anywhere for lunch or for dinner?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: On Saturday, around 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening, a person called Lazo Trojan came, we were locked up in our cells, he unlocked the cells, brought a truck, we went into the truck and he took us to dinner at Utva. And when we finished our dinner, he brought us back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Utva, is that a company?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, it's a company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, were you transferred to another place at some point from the SUP?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When we were brought back from that dinner in Utva, they sent us to the TO across the street from the SUP, about 20 or 30 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, across the street were you put up in a building or in some kind of a garage or something?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: We were put in a garage but it was a little bigger like a room, but a little bit bigger than a room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there inside?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When I was there, there were about 20 or 30 of us but during the night, there were more of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who were there at the TO, did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Ibela was with me, Grga and two of the Bicici brothers who had a pizzeria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean Bicic brothers?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, Bicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the last name is of this Grga, maybe?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I think his last name is Zubak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a police officer before the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he was before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell us whether any of those people were beaten up when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When I was there, one of the two brothers had blood here on his head, his head was bloodied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were at the TO, did anybody come inside to beat these men?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When I was at the TO, nobody hit us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell us when were you released from the TO?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When was I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you freed from the TO?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I was released on Sunday around 10.00 or 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, what happened with your friend who was arrested together with you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My friend was released the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, who told you that you were free to go?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: A member of the special forces came, took me to the SUP, and told me that I was free to go and that I could go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, and where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I went to a building where my mother and father were in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were they in the basement?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They were in the basement because of the shelling, because shells kept falling every little while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during those few days after you were released from the SUP, how frequent was the shelling?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: During those couple of days after my release, in the beginning, for a couple of days, there wasn't any shelling and then there was sporadic shelling for two days and then one day and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, during those initial days, were people leaving Samac, were there any people that you noticed -- that you knew that you noticed were gone?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That day when I came and when I was with my parents, as the days went by, families that had somewhere to go left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, those days after your release, did you notice that there were some people wearing white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: In this building where I was, there were a lot of fighters who were going to the front, to the line, and they had those white bands tied round here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Those were -- they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness said, "around here," Your Honour. Perhaps that could be clarified. He didn't motion anywhere on his body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please point to the place where these white bands were worn, could you indicate with your hand?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The white bands were worn here in that thing on the shirt or the jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Epaulet?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That's where they were tied here on the side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, the Witness indicated his right shoulder, the top of the right shoulder as the place where those white ribbons were attached. Mr. Radic, do you remember the width and the length of those bands?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I think that they were not really so big, they were about this size, they reached more or less down to here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they hung a little bit below the shoulder and it was about 10 or 15 centimetres in length?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell us if you saw any civilians wearing those white bands?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any civilians wearing them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you wear such a band?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your parents?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did you maybe hear of any order that Muslims and Croats had to wear white ribbons when they went out into the street?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: There were a lot of Muslims and Croats with me and I didn't hear anyone say that they had to wear white ribbons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell us whether there was a shortage of bread and milk in that period and did anybody organise for bread and milk to be delivered to Samac citizens?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: In front of the building, immediately in front of the building where we were, milk was distributed and bread to all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and your family receive those supplies?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell us how long did this last?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: This lasted about 10 or 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, did the shops start to work normally again?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The bakeries started to operate and there was bread to be bought in shops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, what was the situation regarding the electricity and water in Bosanski Samac during those days?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The electricity was cut right at the beginning. There was water, there was an artesian well about 100 or 150 metres from our building so when there was no water we could go to there to that well and get some.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell us whether the phones were working in Samac during those days during those few days when the war began?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The telephone worked for only one day. After that, it was all disconnected except for the post office and such places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your telephones in your house also cut off?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the situation with your friends, your acquaintances, Serbs, Croats, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Everybody's phones were cut off regardless of the -- their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later, during the war, was the telephone service restored?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I seek some clarification at this point, Your Honour. The Witness's evidence so far has been that he joined the VRS on the 4th of May, 1993. I asked my learned friend, Mr. Krgovic, to clarify whether this evidence is confined to the period between 16th of April, 1992 and the 4th of May or some other period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Isn't that -- I thought it is in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: From about 16th, 17th April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the following days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought this is the period the witness was covering, from the time that he was arrested, detained, then released and that period, the rest of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think it was my confusion, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness about the first days after the outbreak of the conflict or the situation with the electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were describing the days in April and May 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, later during the war while you were in Bosanski Samac and later towards the end of the war was the telephone service restored?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, it was. We submitted an application to the post office for a telephone line to be installed, not only myself but a sufficient number of families did that and our telephones were connected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the year, you don't have to say the month precisely. When was that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I believe that it was in 1993, I think beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, while you were under arrest, did your family live all the time in their flat?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When I came out of the prison, for a couple of -- for a few months, we lived in that cellar and after that, we went to our flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spent the time in the cellar because of the shelling, nobody forced you out of your flat?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, nobody forced us. While the shells were falling, my father and mother went to their neighbours' place and I went to Miroslav Tadic's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your house close to the front line or to the embankment?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, sort of, perhaps 1 kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your house near the house of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the cellar in the shelter of Miroslav Tadic's house?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: We were in the cafe and in the event of any strong attack, we were going to go down into the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, during 1992, was your father ever arrested?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krgovic, but before the Witness answers that question, can we clarify the name of the cafe? I can make a presumption that I already know what it is, but for the sake of the record, it would be good to have it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, what was the name of Miroslav Tadic's cafe where you used to go?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: It was cafe bar AS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, tell us, was your father arrested during the year of 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My father was arrested on the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: 1992 when the war broke out. We were together in this cellar, two policemen came, asked me what my name was, they asked the same question of my father, and they took him away but they didn't take me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did you find out where your father was eventually taken?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: In this building across the road, there was a police commander, his name was Savo Cancarevic, and my mother and I went early in the morning, it was about 6.00 or 6.30 and we waited for him. My mother asked him what happened and how he was arrested. He replied that they just wanted to question him and if he had been a member of any party and if he didn't have any weapons, that he would be released. He was taken to a secondary school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you find out that he had been taken to the secondary school building?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: We found out immediately, a couple of hours after he had been taken away. We saw a policeman who was there and he told us that my father was in the school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, was there any possibility to -- for you to take some food to your father or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: It all depended on who was on guard, but on several occasions, we managed to bring food to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see your father or your mother while he was in the school building?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, we didn't. No, we couldn't. My mother went there but she was not able to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While your father was in the secondary school building, did he tell you later if he had been beaten or maltreated there?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Nobody touched my father in the school building, nor did he have any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, how much time did your father spend in the school building?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: In the mid-summer, he reported to Zasavica as a butcher and he was taken there and he and a couple of his friends were butchers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did your father stay in Zasavica, can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Altogether, in the school and in Zasavica, between seven and eight months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did you have any opportunity to visit your father in Zasavica, or your mother, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My mother went there several times, and I went two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you go there, did you walk to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: We bicycled there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you enter Zasavica freely or was there any checkpoint at the entry to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Immediately at the entrance point, there was the police there and some of them would let you go through, some of them wouldn't, depended on their mood. But in most cases, they let us go through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went there, did you see where your father was kept?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He and his friend were in a house, it was a furnished house, it was a neat house and there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there water in Zasavica at the time?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, there was. They had a pump and that's where they got the water from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, was Zasavica surrounded by any kind of barbed wire or was there free access to it?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, there was just this checkpoint, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there the police inside the village or the soldiers, did you notice anything like that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: There were no police or army inside the village. Only when they needed something like meat or something then they would come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, was Zasavica ever shelled?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, was it possible for your father to send you some meat from Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, it was. We had some friends there and they brought us meat in cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, when were you served the recruitment notice?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That was in 1993 in January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- were you subjected to any evaluation of your fitness?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I went to the hospital for a medical check-up for my blood test, for them to evaluate whether I was fit for military service and there were many soldiers there of my age who were eligible for recruitment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the usual procedure?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Samac and your father was detained, did you or your mother have work obligation?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, neither my mother nor I had work obligation. I received the summons for recruitment and nobody approached my mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, did any member of your family, your uncle, for example, have work obligation?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My uncle was also a butcher by profession, and he was in charge of doing this job as a butcher for a certain number of companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was never taken in or questioned?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you about the military service, was that the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did your father come home sometime in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My father returned home on the 29th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father tell you that something preceded his release, was he asked to declare whether he wanted to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: His brother, that means my uncle, and his son applied and my father also applied, because my uncle also had two daughters and a wife and they were asking for them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one second, I believe that I heard the Witness say something slightly different than what I see here in the transcript on page 22, line 13. He never actually said that his father applied for exchanges. What I heard that witness said, but maybe my colleague would clarify is that those -- his brother put his name on the list for exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, we'll go question by question. When you said that your uncle and his son wanted to be exchanged and that he put his name on the list, and that he added your father's name on the list, was that right?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other side, --

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: On the other side my uncle wife and two daughters were also asked for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They were in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And what did your father say? Where did he go for the exchange?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They went to the line of separation, that's where the SFOR was, the Russian army, they were there at the line of separation. They asked my father, "Are you going to the other side or are you returning?" My father said that he was returning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, your father returned home?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown document D35/3 ter, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at this document? Mr. Radic, please take your time, look at the document. Could you please tell me whether on the first page, you see your father's name?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Number 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please read that out?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Number 18, Radic, son of Mijo, Mije Radic called Brada.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And what does it say next to it?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Did not decide, he returned -- did not decide, he returned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The name of the person under 18 is Mijo Radic, aka Brada

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me. On page 23, line 24 it states; "Radic, son of Mijo," but the witness actually said "Mijo Radic, called Brada," and that's what it says in the official translation in the English version and I would just like to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. It can be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, Mr. Radic, could you please look at this list very carefully on page 2 and tell me whether any of the people that you know from Samac came back together with your father from the exchange and did not agree to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Number 56, Hasan Pistoljevic, he came back with my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these other people next to their name -- where there is a mark next to their name, number 53, Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I don't know that person. Perhaps I know him but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please take back the document, we won't be needing it anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have one small question for the witness. You said that you were served your mobilisation, your recruitment notice in January 1993. Can you recall whether you received that recruitment notice before or after 29th of January, 1993, which is the date on the document, the exhibit of exchange that we've just looked at, if you could, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you heard Her Honour Judge Williams' question, did you receive this call-up before or after?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I received two envelopes and there it said that it was -- it was the call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this different from the regular call-up in order to serve your regular military term?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: First you need to get your recruitment papers and then you leave that with the persons who are in charge of that, and then you receive separately the actual call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think my question was really specifically as to the date. Do you recall whether you received these -- either one of these two envelopes before your father went to the separation line on 29th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive this call-up document before your father came home or after, if you remember the date? If not, just say so?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I received the recruitment document before and I went for the recruitment procedure and then in the meantime, my father returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then from the recruitment procedure, you came home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I came home. I didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you receive your documents, the call-up to go into the army, when did you go to serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I received my army call-up documents, I think, in April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell me, where did your uncle apply for the exchange when he went; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They went to the Red Cross. That's where you would apply for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your uncle leave Samac then once your father returned?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He went with his son to the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, when your father came back, was he engaged on any work duty anywhere?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: After a couple of days, there was a construction company, my father is a painter by profession, and that was his work duty. If anything needed to be painted, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's clarify, he worked as a butcher. Was your father able to work in the butcher's trade as well as in the house painter's trade? Could you please explain that a little bit because it's a little confusing?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My father, by profession, is a painter, house painter. As a young boy or a young man he worked with another man and he worked on slaughtering sheep and so on so he knows how to do that job as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when your father worked in this construction firm, that was his work duty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell me, during that time while he was working, did your father receive any salary, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My old man or my father did not receive any money but he did receive some assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this assistance in food?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, flour, sugar, oil and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell me, Mr. Radic, did your father work privately as a painter after his work duty, did he have the opportunity to do that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My old man did have the opportunity, but this man who would be requiring his services would ask him to go to his company and to ask first whether he could paint his apartment or so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, Mr. Radic, before you went to serve in the military, did you -- were you engaged in any work duty?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I wasn't engaged in any work duty, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, your uncle, when he applied for the exchange, did he have to give any money for the exchange?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My uncle did not give any money for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell me whether your father or yourself or your family, did you offer to anyone or give money to anyone so that your father could go to the exchange?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, we didn't offer money to anybody, nor did anybody ask for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear in Bosanski Samac at that time before your father left for the exchange and your uncle that money should be given to somebody for them to be placed on the list? And was the name of Miroslav Tadic mentioned in that context?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: We were there at the time, Miroslav Tadic was in charge of exchanges, and he did not take money from anyone for the exchanges neither did anybody offer him money and he didn't ask for money either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear any stories about that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Could you please put that question again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you hear it mentioned or stories being told about him being offered or asking for money for exchanges?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Me and my family did not hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you please tell me whether people, during that time before you went to serve in the military, were people leaving Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes. There were a couple of people who made personal identification cards for money. I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were these people leaving, in which direction, did they go to Serbia or --

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, they all went through Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear whether this was something, this service was something that had to be paid, the service of providing these ID cards?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: What I heard was that in a few instances, yes, this was paid for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did these people go after they went to Serbia, did they go to third countries or did they stay there?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Some people stayed in Serbia, some people went abroad, it depends on where they were able to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think now is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How much time do you need, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take our break and resume at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you continue, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, before the break, we were discussing the work duty and your father's stay in Zasavica so I just want to go back to Zasavica. Could you please tell me before the war, did you used to go to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went there for some matches when they were being held in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what was the ethnicity of the population of that village?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The population was mainly Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask the technical booth to play a short recording, a short video of a few minutes so that the Trial Chamber could see Zasavica. There is no sound, it's just footage of the actual village. From the outside you can see the entrance to Zasavica and several houses. The witness would identify it as the village Zasavica and we would like to submit that as an exhibit. So could the technical booth please play this film.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this turning?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: This is the road to Zasavica and the road straight was the road to Modrica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where this checkpoint with the police was before this bridge or after?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I think it was before the bridge at the very entrance and there was some houses there so it was right next to the first house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise these houses?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, this is Zasavica. On the left side, perhaps the sixth or the seventh house in line was my father's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here on the left side?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't know the house exactly but roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Zasavica look like during the war? Were there any damaged houses there?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I heard when my old man was there that there were not so many damaged houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the technical booth stop now with this footage. I think that we've seen enough. Your Honours, could this document now be given a number, please, if there is no objection from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, there's no objection but could the record reflect that the date on the tape we've just seen was the 3rd of October, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that's clearly visible. Yes, can I have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next number for this exhibit is D142/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, what you just saw, this footage, was Zasavica look like the same at the time in 1992 when you went to visit your father?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Ninety-five per cent it looked the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, you mentioned during your previous testimony that sometime in May 1993, you went to military service. Where did you spend most of the time? I would like to know particularly about the period before the end of December 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I returned on the 6th of May from Bijeljina, I came to the command post. For a certain period of time, I was at the border between Croatia and Bosnia and then I was transferred for about a month or two at the command post. After that, I was transferred to the line, to the front line Grebnice and that is where I spent the whole time until the war ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, while you were in the military, where did you spend most of your breaks? Did you spend the nights at home?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, I spent the time at my parents' and during my free time, I went to Miroslav Tadic's cafe, whenever I had free time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back briefly to 1992 because I omitted to ask you something. Did you, perhaps, in the course of 1992 hear of an order for all the Croats to be arrested and to be placed on vital features both in the town and in the villages?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I have never heard of such -- I never heard of such an order, including my whole family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the document P71 ter to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, tell me, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No. This is the first time that I see it and I've never heard of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, on the 15th or 16th of May, were you in Bosanski Samac, you and your family?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any member of your family -- was any member of your family, your uncle or any of your relatives arrested at the time?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Usher. I don't need this document anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, during those days that you were in Bosanski Samac before your military service, could you listen to Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, whenever there was electricity, we did listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on the air regularly?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, regularly but only when we had electricity and then we listened to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the kind of programme broadcast? Have you ever heard a statement or did you hear at any time that Simo Zaric or -- spoke on the radio?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, there were only comments on the events on the lines and things like that, but Simo Zaric and Blagoje Simic I've never heard speaking on the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Simo Zaric insulting Croats and Muslims over the radio, that he used abusive language?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Simo Zaric never insulted anyone, instead, he helped a lot, both to the Croats and the Muslims and that was not only that I said, many people have said that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, tell us, how long have you known Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I have known Miroslav Tadic some -- for some 15 or 16 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, did you frequent the AS cafe?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, because I was a younger boy and I did go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radic, in those days, did you ever heard of the existence of a so-called 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I heard there were people from all three ethnicities, Croats, Muslims and Serbs in that detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I wasn't a member of none of the units before I received a call-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about your father?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He didn't -- he wasn't a member either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, do you know where was the headquarters of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Across the road from a neighbour Tadic in the Sit factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, in those days, you frequented the AS Cafe and tell me were there any rooms inside the cafe that were off limits and that were closed for other patrons?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, there were no such rooms, everything was accessible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, what was the ethnic composition of the cafe patrons?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: All ethnicities were there, Croats, Muslims and Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that continue during the war as well?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, both during the war and after the war, everything remained the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, I would like to ask you something about your family. You mentioned in your previous testimony that your father had three sisters, did they live in Bosanski Samac before the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, two of them lived in Samac and one was married in Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did she spend the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: In the beginning, she came -- at the beginning of the war, she came to Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she spend the whole time of the war in Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other sisters?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They were also in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have families?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they still living in Samac nowadays? During the war or more precisely until the end of December 1993, were they forcibly evicted from their flats?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: These two sisters were not evicted, but the third one who was married in Gradacac, she was given a flat where she was allowed to stay with her daughters while the situation was as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Here on page 35 line 3, there are actually two questions that were posed to the witness. "Are they still living in Samac now a days?" But it looks that we don't have the answer to the question in the record, the witness actually did give his answer but maybe it should be posed again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can -- I'm sure counsel can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me just ask you because we -- there is something unclear in the transcript, I will repeat the question. You said your father had three sisters?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, three sisters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two of them, before the war, lived in Samac, the whole time?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do they still live in Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: These two sisters live in Samac and the third sister was given a flat in Gradacac, but she occasionally comes to Samac to visit her daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she spend the whole time of the war in Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she reside with any of her sisters?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, she did, and in the meantime she got her own flat. That was a kind of temporary residence and the other two sisters had their own flats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this temporary residence?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: In an apartment block, she was given a flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She is a Croat?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Radic, did any of your father's sisters was evicted from her flat during the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: None of them were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While your father was detained, did you ever leave your flat?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, we stayed there until the end of the war, after the war, and we still live in that same flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, what happened with your uncle's property after he left Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The property of my uncle was hit by a missile and the house was demolished, not altogether but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your uncle is still alive, I understand?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he die after he left Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: A few months after he had been exchanged he had some stomach pains, he had undergone surgery and he never woke up after the surgery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you said that you have known Miroslav Tadic for a long time. Do you know, as much as you know and heard, did Miroslav Tadic force any Muslim or Croat to leave Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Never. He never forced anyone. If he was able to help anyone, he did help, but he never forced anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, through your contacts with Miroslav Tadic and his attitude towards you and your family, did you notice any discriminatory attitude or intolerance towards you as Croats?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Not only in my case, but that applies to all ethnicities, Miroslav Tadic behaved correctly. He helped us. He provided food and water for us. He never uttered an abusive word and he never insulted us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard or seen, yourself, that he treated other non-Serbs in a discriminatory manner, that he degraded them or abused them?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I've never heard any such thing, nor were there any rumours to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished my examination. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel wishes to ask this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. On behalf of Mr. Pantelic, he didn't want to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Cross-examination by the Prosecution, if any. Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, my name is David Re from the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you some questions; do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence was that you've known Miroslav Tadic for 16 or 17 years. You must know him fairly well then.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, I know very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a relative of yours or your family's?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, we are neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a friend or is he a friend of your parents?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He is the friend of our whole household.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A very good friend of your whole household?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: A very good one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were young, did you call him uncle?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your parents customers of his at Cafe As before, during or after the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, no. My father didn't go to places like this, restaurants and things, and my mother too, and -- but I did go there during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work for Mr. Tadic during the war in his Cafe As?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there were no rooms off limit, does that -- did you mean that there were no rooms off limit in his cafe to you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, no. All rooms in the cafe were accessible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The cafe of course is connected to his house or his apartment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The cafe has a room where cards were played and as far as that is concerned, I can claim that there were no off-limit rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The cafe is connected to his apartment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, upstairs, but in the cafe, whenever I went there, no rooms were closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the access to his house or his apartment upstairs. Was his apartment upstairs accessible at the time you were there at the cafe; that is, could you go through the cafe upstairs to his house without obstruction?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: While I was there, whenever I say -- I was there once, my old man wanted to paint something in the neighbour's house and I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this is -- I think this is confusing the witness. I suppose that the question was whether the apartment was accessible from the cafe and I think that it wasn't translated properly so we have to clarify or not now or maybe after the cross-examination but I think this was due to an incorrect translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can certainly clarify it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Radic, about the access from the cafe to Mr. Tadic's apartment upstairs. Do you understand that, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand now that's what I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: You asked me whether the cafe is connected to the house, if I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again in a different way. You've agreed that the cafe was connected to the house. What I'm asking you now is in the time you went to the cafe, were you able to go from the cafe to the apartment upstairs without obstruction? Were you able to just walk from the cafe up the stairs to his apartment?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't when there were two entrances, one to the cafe and one to the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the entrance to the house was locked to customers, that is customers couldn't go from the cafe upstairs to the apartment?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The guests were not locked up at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his house or his apartment upstairs off limits to customers in the cafe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Re. I think for clarity on line 12, the answer is recorded as, "The guests were not locked up at all." Maybe you could clarify whether that, in fact, was what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard what Her Honour Judge Williams just said. Did you say, Mr. Radic, that "the guests were not locked up at all" or is that a mistranslation?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The guests were in the cafe and not in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is was Mr. Tadic's apartment upstairs off limits to the customers in the cafe? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, because I had the opportunity to go up there when I needed something so it wasn't closed off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the accused Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you known Mr. Simo Zaric for?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I have known him since I was a boy and so I've known him during the war. I've known him for long enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do your parents also know Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they also friends with Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they are in good relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... A friend of Mr. Zaric. Let us make some distinction, because he knows Mr. Zaric being a friend is a bit different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't see anything wrong with the question and the Prosecution can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your parents are in good relations with Mr. Zaric, meaning they're friends with Mr. Zaric, are you a friend of Mr. Zaric's?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, I am. During the war -- before the war, I was 16 or 17 years old. When the war began I was 18. During the war, I got to know Mr. Zaric even better, I knew him before the war, but during the war, I got to know him better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get to know him during the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I knew him in a good light through socialising with him, through help and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you just expand upon that, please, what do you mean by socialising with him and through help? What sort of things did you and Mr. Zaric do together during the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: We socialised, we played billiards, we celebrated birthdays and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about when you said a moment ago "through help," what did you mean you knew him through help during the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, he wouldn't let anybody pick on me as a Croat. He was also well-meaning towards other people and he didn't do any harm to me or to my family and that's why I think he was good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what official position did he hold during the war when you were socialising with him, celebrating birthdays and so on and playing billiards?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: After the war, I was on good terms with him, I knew him also during the war. He wouldn't let anyone pick on me or attack me because I did have some problems, certain people would pick on me, hit me, members of the army, and Mr. Tadic and Mr. Zaric always wouldn't let them pick on me so I meant that in that sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, of course, had a high official position in Bosanski Samac during the war, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I heard -- I did hear that he had -- I didn't hear that he had a high position. I heard that Simo Zaric was in the army, but I'm not really all that familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew, of course, that Mr. Tadic had a high official position in the town, I think, as you said he was in charge of the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were quite fortunate in having these two people with official positions in a position to protect you, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I was very lucky with them, to be on good terms with them and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know or do you know Simo Zaric's son?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I do. His son and I went to school together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you or were you friends with his son?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: His son and I went to school together for eight years and we know each other very well to this very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Re, maybe we should clarify which one of Mr. Zaric's sons we're talking about here, okay?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which son we're talking about, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Mirel Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
