utterances.text: And did you remain friends with Mirel Zaric during the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the army with you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, we were not together in the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the army at all or did he remain behind?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes. He was in the army for a while, just like I was, and then he went to school or the university or whoever was able to do anything like that so everything ended quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about Dr. Blagoje Simic, do you know Dr. Blagoje Simic sitting over there?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic I know so-so from just seeing him around like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do your parents know Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Maybe also by sight but I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from your father, mother, and your father's three sisters, as of April 1992, did you have any other relatives living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That's all the family that I had in Samac. I didn't have anyone else in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father's third sister from Gradacac, did she have a husband?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the person whose flat she moved into when she came to Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but when everything stablised itself, when all the apartments were stablised, she returned the apartment to the person who was there, got his apartment back as soon as he came back after the war. So she didn't spend a long time in that apartment, it was only until the owner came and she left as soon as she got her own apartment in Gradacac. Now she's living privately and paying rent because her apartment in Gradacac was also occupied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the person whose apartment it was; in other words, whose apartment was it that she moved into?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because I didn't have an opportunity to ask that because I was involved with my own affairs. I went to the frontline and I was concerned saving my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Her Serb husband, did he come with her to Samac and move into that apartment?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he came. I don't know how long he was over there during the war, he was sent away from Gradacac through some line or some forest. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the VRS during the war when your father's sister was living in the apartment in Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. He was not a member of any army or any party. He worked in a large company in Gradacac and he wasn't in any army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Re, maybe you should clarify on page 45, line 2, the answer to your question concerning the Serb husband of the Witness' aunt, you asked whether he came with her to Samac and move into that apartment and the answer was "no, he came," so it doesn't really tell us too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did your aunt's husband come to the apartment in Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He came maybe -- I don't know exactly, maybe it was after seven or eight months, something like that. It's not quite precise, but approximately then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it was. Yes, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your father's two other sisters, did they have husbands during the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, both of my aunts were married.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of their husbands?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: One of them was a Serb and the other was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one whose husband was a Serb, did he go away to war in the army or did he remain behind in Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your aunt whose husband was a Serb, did he remain in Samac during the war or did he go to -- go in the army?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: This aunt of mine, her husband and my older cousin both went to the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the Bosnian Serb army, was it?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, I -- I was in that army as well. There were all kinds of people there, not only Serbs, there were Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said. The interpreters didn't catch all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, can you just repeat your last answer? I asked you whether your aunt's husband and older cousin went into the Bosnian Serb army, just repeat your answer to that, please.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: This aunt whose husband came from Gradacac, is that the one you mean or the other two aunts, one of whose husbands is a Serb? Could you please clarify that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had three aunts, two married to Serbs one married to a Croat. One was in Samac and married to a Serb?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about her husband.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did go to the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the VRS?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your older cousin, is that a son?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We are first cousins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he regard himself as a Croat or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, he considered himself a Serb, that's what they said, but unfortunately for him, he didn't spend a long time in the army and he was killed on the line and he was 20 or 21 when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your third aunt, the one who was married to a Croat? What did he do during the war, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Her husband went across to the Croatian side and she stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against this line, but it's not clear, the part, the interpreter said that they did not hear the questions went in another direction and the witness did not actually repeat what he said. The sentence that he said, I cannot ask that question, the witness said something, but the questions are now going in a completely different direction. What he said is that he was talking about the ethnic composition of the army of Bosnian Serbs, this is what he said in that one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That, however, was not my question. My question was whether the husband went to war, there was nothing about the ethnic composition of the army. My friend can clarify that in re-examination if he wishes so it's not part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the instruction of the Trial Chamber was for the witness to repeat his answer and not the line or the case of the Prosecution. We did not get what the Trial Chamber requested and it's already gone past but it is something we will clarify in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you will take it up in re-examination. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were detained on the 16th of April by, you said, special police, they took your money from you. Did you get your money back from them?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They did not return the money to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much money did they take?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I didn't have a lot of money, 70 or 80 marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were locked up, I wasn't quite sure what you said about who you saw in the police station. You said you saw some police on duty, were those police -- or police had gone to work, were those police who were locked up, is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, they were there with me together in that cell, the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those police officers non-Serbs, that is Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, in that sense. They were Muslims, the people who worked there and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The cells you were in, they filled up during that day and the next day, didn't they, with people brought in?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When I was there, those two cells had about 10 or 15 of us in each cell. There was one bed in each cell and there was a corridor next to the two cells and there were about 7, 8 or 10 people there until we went to the TO. Once we went to the TO, there were as many of us there as there were for as long as I was there. Then when I went, I guess during the time I was there, no more people came for that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever charged with committing a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I never was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever brought to court as a result of your detention?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These guards came and took people out of the cells at intervals, for interrogation, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, they -- those two Serbians took me and took me upstairs and when the interrogation was finished, they brought me back to the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards took other prisoners out of the cells for interrogation too, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: While I was there, no. I was maybe there and another man, perhaps, I don't know his name, but other than that, nobody else went for interrogation for as long as I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your parents know that you were detained in the SUP and the TO for those few days in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: They found out the next day, so they only found out on Saturday. They heard from friends that I was seen at the SUP so they heard about it on Saturday and I was detained on Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which friends they heard from that you were detained in the SUP or TO?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Probably from the soldiers who were there, people who were walking around. I don't know. Because a lot of people knew me and I was on good terms with all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Simo Zaric at either the SUP or the TO?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I didn't see Simo Zaric neither on Thursday or Friday or Saturday or Sunday at the SUP or at the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the people who were detained there with you tell you that they had seen or spoken to Mr. Zaric at the SUP or the TO?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I didn't hear that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Miroslav Tadic, did you see Mr. Miroslav Tadic at the SUP or the TO when you were detained there in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I didn't see him either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the prisoners or detainees tell you that they had seen or heard Miroslav Tadic at the SUP or TO during those few days?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about that. There were -- there was talk -- there was no talk about either Simo Zaric or Miroslav Tadic as far as I know, they didn't talk about that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Miroslav Tadic knew that you were imprisoned for those few days in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether he was there or whether he knew, but I assume that it's possible that he knew because I came on the -- the day, Thursday to Friday, so it's possible but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever given any reasons for your release?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, the reasons were -- the reasons for my release were because I wasn't guilty and because I was on the street at a wrong time and there were no other provocations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you whether anyone gave you reasons for your release. Did anyone tell you where you were being released?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, a man from Serbia came. I don't know his name, but I would like to know his name. He came to the TO to fetch me. He took me outside, he put his arm around my shoulders and he said, "Young man, come with me to the SUP," and he added, "You are not guilty of anything so you just nicely go back home so if anyone stops you in the street you just can say to them that it was me who released you," and that is how I was released from the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether your parents spoke to Miroslav Tadic about having you released from the SUP or the TO?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I don't know that precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic showed you a document, it was P71 which was an order of the Crisis Staff ordering Croats to be isolated and taken to vital facilities dated the 15th of May, 1992. Do you remember him showing you a document maybe a half an hour ago?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Another document? You mean the other document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown again so that we don't waste time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have P71 in front of you, Mr. Radic, that's the document ordering the isolation of Croats in Samac.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That was not isolation of Croats, that referred to those who were in the HDZ party or who had weapons. They remained in the school and the others had work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you can just read the words under decision where it says "All people of Croatian nationality on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac," it doesn't say anywhere there HDZ, does it?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I'm just telling you that those who were members of the party -- I don't know if they had to or not, but as for the rest, that isn't it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence when Mr. Krgovic showed you that document was, you said something to the effect of "No member of my family was arrested at the time." That was what you said. Now, that document's dated the 15th of May, your other evidence was that your father was arrested on the 1st of June, 1992 which is only two weeks later. When you said no member of my family was arrested at the time, do you mean -- just let me finish -- did you mean around that day being the 15th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, my father was taken for questioning. He asked him if he had questions and this -- weapons and this and that and nothing else happened and after that, he was transferred to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'm only asking you about your answer to a question Mr. Krgovic asked you in relation to that document and that no members of your family were arrested at the time. Your evidence was your father was arrested on the 1st of June, 1992 and taken to the high school. When you said, "No member of my family was arrested at the time," did you mean at the time as in around those days, around the 15th of May? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date. I was imprisoned and I was under the shock and I cannot exactly recall the day when this all happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying. Your earlier evidence was that your father as arrested on the 1st of June, 1992. You stand by that evidence, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He was taken to this school that was in mid-summer when he was transferred to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father -- I withdraw that I'll start again. Some armed men came to your house and took your father away, he was not free to leave, was he? He had to go with them.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Not armed men but the police came to take him, asked him for his full name and then took him to the school, asked him if he was member of any party, and the next morning, my mother and I went there and said -- and that's what had happened. They told my mother and myself that if he wasn't guilty of being member of any party, he would be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, please to concentrate on the question I'm asking and answer that one. Your father was arrested, he was not free to leave the company of those police officers, was he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No. The policemen came nicely and took him nicely away. They didn't hit him nor force him, they just told him nicely that an order was issued for him to be taken in. They behaved in a correct way. They knew my father, and didn't say anything apart from that. So nobody hit him or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I didn't ask you about what they did to him so can you please confine your answers to the question I'm asking you. He was not free to leave because he was under arrest, it's a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, is it not clear when the witness said they just told him nicely that an order was issued for him to be taken in so the police were acting on that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I take Your Honour's point, I won't pursue that any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, your father was not a member of any political party, was he? Just, please, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he couldn't have been guilty of being a member of any party, could he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: In the terms that you are putting it, my father was reported by some neighbours of ours that he was this and that and that is why he was picked up. It all started from our neighbours, but I don't know which neighbours exactly, but that was rumour that he was tipped off by a neighbour and that is why the police came to take him in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence was, "They told my mother and myself that he wasn't guilty of being a member of any party, he would be released." My question was simply your father wasn't a member of any party so he couldn't have been guilty of being a member of a party, could he? That's all I'm asking you based on what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That's what I told you and I have nothing else to add and I don't know, myself, how it all went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father was detained without charge or trial at the high school, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was he in the high school for?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, he went there on the 1st of June and sometime in mid-summer, I don't know exactly, he was transferred or he was not transferred, in fact, because they needed a butcher over there, and he applied for that job because later, a conclusion was adopted or made that my father wasn't guilty of anything at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, please just answer the question. I asked you how long he was there for, that's all. You said mid-summer, is that July, is that August, just doing the best you can?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly because in total, he spent in the school and in the Zasavica seven or eight months and I cannot say exactly it was a month or a month and a half. My mother and I were in a shock and we didn't know exactly so I think it's one month or month and a half, depends, maybe end of August, I don't know exactly. So all in all, in Zasavica and in the school, he spent between seven and eight months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He wasn't free to leave the high school, was he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he wasn't because somebody was obstructing this procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was guarded by armed guards, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that was the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they took him to Zasavica, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He wasn't free to leave Zasavica when he was working there as a butcher either, was he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, he worked there until exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was working there as a butcher, he was not free to leave it, was he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father was taken from the high school to Zasavica to work as a butcher. For as long as he worked there as a butcher, he was not free to leave Zasavica, was he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he voluntarily applied to go to Zasavica. That was his job that he performed there and he was waiting there to be exchanged. He was free to walk around the village but he couldn't leave the village. Everything was free, not only for him, but for other people who were there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just that none of them could leave Zasavica, could they?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, because they had this work obligation and they were needed there because butchers were scarce and they worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father could not have left Zasavica and gone home and lived in your place in Bosanski Samac while he was doing his work obligation there, could he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, until exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He couldn't work as a butcher in Zasavica during the day and come home to Samac, a few kilometres away, at night, could he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly that's how it was. I don't know on whose orders it was. I only know that he was in Zasavica but aside from that, I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you know, your father wasn't a criminal, was he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He hadn't committed any offences, had he?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your uncle, was he a criminal?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had he committed any offences that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While your father was detained in the SUP, did he tell you what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell anything. Whoever ordered that, ordered that in Zasavica. He didn't have any problems. They were waiting for exchange. The main thing was that nobody provoked him, beat him, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one second because I have noticed something just to assist my learned colleague. The answer was here on page 57 line 15, no he didn't tell anything. Whoever ordered that, ordered that, and that's where the point mark should be and then he -- it was another word in Zasavica he didn't have any problems. In this way it doesn't make much sense. It seems that someone from Zasavica ordered something to the police or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I asked him about the SUP, I don't know where Zasavica comes from. I can ask again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think his evidence in chief was clear on that, that he wasn't ill-treated in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking him about Zasavica, I don't know where Zasavica comes from I only asked him about the SUP. The transcript says Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah, you can go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'm only asking you now about the high school, please only answer the question about the high school, nothing else. When your father was detained in the high school, do you know whether he went out to work during the day and came back to the high school in the afternoon or night?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, but some people went out of the school to do their job during the day, and in the night they went back to school, depended on which kind of craft skills were required until it became necessary for people to go to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify that, are you saying you don't know whether your father was one of those people who left during the day to work and came back at night?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I can tell you, but I only know that now, it depended whether somebody's painting skills were needed. As I told you, my old man used to do painting works and after that, he would return to school. That's all I know and as for the rest, I wouldn't be able to reply to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be crystal clear, your father told you that he went out in the day to do painting and came back to the school at night? I just want to clarify that one point.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told Mr. Krgovic, when he asked you some questions, about you and your mother trying to visit your father in Zasavica and you said, "In most cases, they let us through." You said you managed to get to go there two or three times. How many times did you try to visit your father in Zasavica but were turned away?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, I already said it all depended on the police. In 70 or 80 or maybe 90 per cent of the cases they let us through and 10 per cent they didn't let us through, it all depended in which mood they were or something like that. Maybe my mother was turned away not more than once or twice or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about you, were you ever turned away when you tried to visit your father in Zasavica? If yes, how many times?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought the explanation was clear that there were times when he was turned away, maybe 10 per cent which depended on the mood of the police or the guards. So why do you want the exact number of times?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't want the exact number, the figures just quite add up, he said two to three times or ten per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But it's clear that he can't remember exactly which times the point is more. They were allowed more than they weren't allowed. But on most occasions they were allowed. On some occasions which were fewer occasions, they were not allowed to see him. I think this is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I won't take that any further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Zasavica, -- I'll start again. You saw the video and I think you pointed out where you thought your father's house was. When you went to see him, did you go straight to see him and stay with him or did you do other things in the village?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I just went directly to the house where he was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was about, I think on the video, maybe 70 metres or so inside the road as it turns to the left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, when you start from the bridge and then a row of houses and I think it was the sixth house on the left-hand side. I cannot say exactly now. I am not 100 per cent sure, but my mother and I went to this house when my father and his colleague were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to visit him, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, we were allowed to stay. Nobody told us, "You can stay half an hour, one hour, two hours," we could stay for as long as we wanted without any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about the two or three times you actually went to see him there, from memory, how long did you stay with him on those two or three occasions?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Approximately between one and two hours because it was difficult for me to be there. I wanted to stay as short as possible, but once I realised that he was safe, and that there were no problems, it was a relief for my mother and myself. The first time we saw how he was faring, we didn't -- we didn't worry too much after that. We saw that he was in a safe place, that nobody is ill -- was ill treating-him, there were no provocations and that everything was in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I just want to summarise your evidence on your visits to Zasavica, that is, you went there two or three times, you went straight to his house which was the sixth or seventh house in from turning the road, you stayed there for maybe one to two hours and you stayed there and -- left and went straight out; is that correct? Is that your evidence about your visits to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your mother, in response to questions from Mr. Krgovic, didn't have a work obligation during the war. What was her state of health during the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: My mother is a rather plumpy person. She was in good health. She couldn't work -- she could work but nobody asked her to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence to Mr. Krgovic when he asked you questions about Mr. Miroslav Tadic was that no one paid him any money to leave Samac on an exchange. You, of course, weren't with Mr. Tadic during negotiations for people to get on exchange lists, were you?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I wasn't present, but there were a lot of people in my street and everywhere and everybody talked and said that Mr. Tadic never took money from anyone for exchange. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't what I was asking you. I'm asking you about your own personal experiences. You also didn't go to any exchanges with Mr. Tadic, did you; just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to take shelter in Mr. Tadic's cafe during the war after your release from the TO? How was that arranged?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When we returned from the cellar, my mother and father and I came, the shells were falling, my father and mother went to find shelter at one of our neighbours and I went to this cafe while the shelling was in progress. I fell into it, I bruised my hands and they put bandages on my hands and they -- I went back after everything was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Mr. Tadic's cellar for?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Until the danger was over. I was there, we ate there in the evening as well, I went home, my parents were at home, we were always there whenever it was necessary. I was there and my mother and father were at a neighbours' across the street they didn't come with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out is how long you spent in the cellar, was it hours, days, months, weeks, what was it?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: When the shells were falling, this would be for a couple of hours, when it was dangerous during the shelling, then I would stay a little bit longer to see that the shelling wouldn't begin again and so that I wouldn't need to escape again. So I would stay there for a few hours and when everything calmed down, I would go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often did you go to Mr. Tadic's cellar, was it every day, every week, every month, between what periods?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: It depends. When I had some free time, that's when I would go, when I didn't have any free time, we were all there, we would keep each other company, that was where it was the safest for us, not only for me but for all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking about you. How often did you go to Mr. Tadic's cellar was it every time it was shelled?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting my learned friend but the Witness already replied in the previous answer when the -- when there was shelling, that's when I would go. So he already specified the time. And to the previous question of the Prosecutor also he replied.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm merely trying to find out how often -- when the shelling was, was it every day was it every week, was it every month, that's all I want to know. It wasn't quite answered. There are two things that I can't quite make sense of. I'm just asking the witness did you go every time it was shelled, was it shelled every day, every week or every second day, when? It's just unclear at the moment. That's all I'm trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think you can find out from the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, do you understand, I just want to know, we just want to know how often you went to the cellar. Was it every day, was it being shelled every day or was it every second day or every third day? That's all I want to know and for how long, was it for April until the next year or when so just those two things?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I went only when the shells were falling. When I had free time, I was there. We were in the cellar once, we were for sometime here and there but whenever we were there, I would go to my neighbour's Miroslav Tadic's. I was there when I had time off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were the shells falling that you had to take shelter in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: At one point, there was shelling more frequently, one, two or three days. Then for 10, 15 or 20 days, there would be no danger then again it would begin. Perhaps it would not be 10 days in a row it would be 2 or 3 days and then it would stop or 3 or 4 days and then it would stop so when I was there, I would go there but when there was no shelling, then I would be in my apartment and that's where I would be more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said there were other people in the cellar when the shelling was occurring, who were these other people?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: There were people who happened to be on the street, I know those people, I don't know everybody's name but we were all there together. Nobody was separate. Always somebody would be going somewhere and they would happen to be on the street and then they would come to the neighbour, Miroslav Tadic's or to the cafe and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that you received your recruitment papers in January 1993 while your father was in Zasavica. Did you tell your father that you had received your work -- your recruitment papers before he left Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: I didn't tell that to my father, but my father heard that from the other side, that I had received the recruitment papers and I said that I would go and he said thank God that you are going to go because we stayed behind here and we plan to stay. That's why I reported to the recruitment, because I had the right not to go but I decided to go and this is how my father accepted it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are taking our break, Mr. Re. Yes. And we shall resume our proceedings at 1805. --- Break taken at 5.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, just before the break, you said that your father had heard from the other side that you'd received the recruitment papers, you said you'd go and he said, "Thank God you're going to go because we stayed behind here and we plan to stay." That's what you said just before the break. Do you mean by that that your going to fight -- your joining the VRS enabled your father to stay behind in Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That's what he said so there's nothing much for me to say about that. I received this summons for the army, I went to the army, I came back from the army, and I'm still living there to this very day and there are no problems at all. I remained living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father, I think you said he had a private business, was it a private business as a painter in Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, he was a painter from before the war, that was his profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he own business premises before the war from which he conducted his painting business?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, it wasn't really a major business, it was -- we had a garage, that's where the tools were kept and everything. It wasn't some big company or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a garage he owned or rented?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, no, it was our garage, just made from boards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father have any employees in his painting business?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father have any people working for him in this painting business he had before the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No. He had a couple of assistants, one or two of them, if there was a bigger job, but if it was a small job, it depends if there was a -- if it was a job in a house, then two of them would go, if it was an apartment, then one person would go. He had assistants but he was the craftsman so without him, nothing could be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he would subcontract people if -- when needed, that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, when he needed help, then -- but he had one person who was there permanently but if needed, then somebody would come to earn some extra money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, did your father have contracts or did your father do painting work for the local government authorities?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No. He worked mainly in households or cafes or restaurants and so on. He worked a lot in the villages, but he never did anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do work for Miroslav Tadic, Simo Zaric, or Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He did some painting for Simo Zaric and Blagoje Simic, no, for Miroslav Tadic, but he worked for money. They paid for everything that he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that before, during or after the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Before the war and during the war were these jobs done, specially when my father was in the exchange. Mr. Miroslav Tadic called him, he was there on work duty, to paint something for him, a room or something. He gave him food, he gave him drink and he paid him so it wasn't anything like that whereas in other cases, others would just say thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had a garage. Did your father -- or did your parents own a house or a flat in Samac?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, we had an apartment in Samac and we have a weekend house in Ledenice, something like that and the garage was something that we just made from planks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Ledenice?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Ledenice is next to Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the garage?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: The garage was in Samac right next to our apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe my colleague would like to take a look at the transcript on page 67 -- now it's all right. Now it's all right, it's been replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your parents keep the garage, their apartment, and their weekender in Ledenice after the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes. The garage is not big and in Ledenice is the -- that's where the property is of my mother so that was the land where the house was built before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The apartment, did your parents keep your apartment after the war -- during and after the war?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes. We kept it during the war and we're in that apartment now. And during the weekend my mother and father --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, this is a problem you keep repeating the question sometimes. I mean, this question of the apartment, them living in that apartment during the war and up to now has been stated I think three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My memory has failed me on that particular point, Your Honour, I don't have the transcript. I don't have the benefit of the transcript in front of me as I ask the question. I couldn't remember that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, when did your father resume his private painting business?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He resumed it during the war and after the war and he's doing the same kind of work now. There isn't really that much work right now, but there is some work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier when I asked you that you knew Mr. Zaric during the war playing billiards with him and socialising with him and I think you said in the army, did you serve in the army with Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, we were not in the army together, but during the war, we were there and we socialised because I was in Grebnice so we knew each other. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we move into private session for just one moment so I can put the name of a person to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, we are in open session. Re-examined by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radic, I'm going to ask you a few more questions relating to your responses to the Prosecutor during cross-examination. Mr. Radic, the Prosecutor asked you whether you were friends with Mr. Miroslav Tadic and you explained that you socialised, you were neighbours, and friends and that Miroslav Tadic helped you and your family so I'm asking you now: Did you notice whether Miroslav Tadic helped other people of Muslim or Croat ethnicity who were not his friends?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He helped me and those Muslims. Miroslav Tadic did not do a bad turn to anyone or said anything bad to anyone. If he knew a person or if he didn't know a person, he would help them if he was able to help them. As far as I know, he never did anything that would harm a person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about your engagement in the army of Republika Srpska and he asked you a question stating: Did you serve in the Serbian army? And then you responded, you started to reply but this was not recorded in the transcript. You said that it was not only the Serb army so could you please continue with your answer?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: It wasn't a Serb army when I was there. When I was in Bijeljina and then returned, I was the only Croat, I was the only Croat as far as ethnicity was concerned and the rest was Serbs, but when I came back to Samac on the 6th of May -- I went on the 4th, came back on the 6th to be in my units with my people, and when I was there in the command and on the border, I was transferred to Grebnice, to the frontline, and I went there to the trenches together with Muslims and Croats and Serbs and we were all together in one trench.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you when he mentioned the detention of your father and he asked you about your uncle and he said -- he asked you that your uncle, whether he was a criminal or was he suspected of anything. Was he ever arrested or imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No, he was never arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, the Prosecutor asked you about your father, whether your father committed any criminal act, whether he had weapons, whether he was a member of any party and he asked you and you replied to the question whether your father was ever tried or whether there were any criminal charges brought against your father. Now, I'm asking you: Was your father ever suspected of bearing arms or taking part in any formations?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or was he possibly suspected of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: He was never suspected of anything like that and he never committed any kind of criminal act. He was never in any political party and in particular, he never had any weapons. It's possible that a neighbour reported him. That's probably what it was all about. But he never did anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: That was confirmed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you are forgetting to pause. The interpreters are having a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to ask you from the beginning. At the end, was it determined that your father did not commit any criminal act and that he never had any weapons or participated in armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: Dario Radic
utterances.text: Yes, that was determined and resolved. My old man is absolutely not guilty. He did not commit any criminal act or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, when the Prosecutor asked you about Zasavica and he asked you to describe to him when you entered Zasavica, whether you went directly to your father or you didn't go to Zasavica in -- around Zasavica and you described those conditions. I'm asking you now did your father tell you how or did you -- did he ever complain about the conditions of life in the village of Zasavica which were there at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. I didn't ask anything about the conditions in Zasavica. That was covered in chief. I only asked about how long he went there for and coming and going. That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, you can't extend your examination-in-chief now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic, for giving evidence. We are finished with you. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the next witness on the schedule is the accused, Miroslav Tadic. I am ready to begin, although I wanted to propose, since we have half an hour left, that we begin with Mr. Tadic tomorrow and that maybe we can deal with some legal issues right now, but if the Chamber wishes, we can start. I wanted to inform the Chamber namely about the witnesses. You were informed about a witness who did not testify during the depositions and we decided to give up on that witness. There is another witness regarding -- in accordance with Rule 92 bis I also wanted to ask for the instructions of the Chamber regarding our demographic expertise. I don't know whether this is the time to deal with that or do you wish us to start with Mr. Tadic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think we will deal with the procedural issues we have. We can start hearing the evidence of the accused tomorrow. So you can proceed with the matters you wanted to raise. Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On behalf of Miroslav Tadic's Defence I wanted to inform the Chamber you received the motion informing you or -- of the officer who did the depositions about the fact that one of the witnesses will not appear, that is witness with initials DW 5/3. The gist of the matter is that this witness, even though we spoke with him several times, and he promised that he would come to Belgrade, because of some circumstances that he didn't want to discuss with me too much, he said in any case that he did not wish to leave the territory of Samac and did not wish to testify. That is why we are giving up this witness. I did not wish to exert any pressure even though during the weekend, myself and my colleague Mr. Pisarevic tried - who knows his son very well - to talk to this witness and to try to influence him so that he would still come and testify. But we are not going to ask this witness to testify. And also, we will not ask Witness Zika Krunic to give us a statement under Rule 92 bis. This is a witness under number 35 and he was to testify under Rule 92 bis. We cannot get in touch with this witness, namely he told me that because of his obligations as an investigating judge, he is not able to leave the territory where he's working and I could not guarantee to him that he would not be invited for cross-examination. He said that he could only sign a statement for me so in that sense, I do not wish to call this witness on behalf of Tadic's Defence. There is another technical problem with a witness who was to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What was his name because I'm looking on the list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is Witness Zika Krunic he was originally planned to give a deposition in the pre-trial procedure. He is an investigative judge from Bijeljina. But by your decision, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you said that his testimony be given based on the 92 bis, but he said that due to his other commitments, he cannot leave his work place and that is why we gave up on taking this statement; however, other 92 bis statements will be taken as instructed on the 18th of February. I have another technical problem concerning the testimony of another witness via videolink. I wouldn't like to mention his name, that's the witness who has a sick wife and who is supposed to come to Belgrade, maybe we can switch to a closed session. My problem is when I asked the secretary of the Chamber could we know approximately at what time during the day we can have this videolink because that person can come to Belgrade in the morning and return in the evening, so within the two weeks, we would like to know in advance some timetable to organise for his arrival or maybe the videolink to have in the early morning hours. So I would kindly ask if I could be notified seven days in advance before the videolink is established so that I can know where we stand and finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just before you go on, the videolink witnesses are scheduled for the week beginning 3rd March and that week we are sitting mornings unless the courtroom is unavailable but otherwise our schedule is for morning sessions. You wanted private session for -- you no longer need it, yes, so what's the other point?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, Your Honours, in compliance with your order regarding the demographic expert study, we appealed to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the occasion of the letter sent by the Census Bureau of BH asking if they can provide this material. We sent this letter to the government on the 10th of January through -- authorised Tribunal liaison officers, however, we did not receive any response and I would simply like to know, based on the instructions by the Chamber, do we -- are we going to wait or are we going to apply Rule 54? I'm afraid that we might enter a stage of the procedure when we must provide this expert study and we would not have received any response from the government. So maybe I can submit to the Court a writ that I had submitted to them and appeal to them officially or should we just wait because we have no other channels of communication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think, since you've been waiting and there's no response, I think the best thing is to apply to the Chamber then we can pick it up from there. Now, finally -- okay. You finish your points before I raise my concerns with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished everything concerning the procedure -- Defence procedure for Miroslav Tadic. What I can conclude -- so the next one to take the witness stand is Mr. Tadic and we have two more witnesses: Mr. Grujicic and another witness. We have two 92 bis depositions that will be taken in Samac on the 18th of February and they will be signed, duly signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: A point for clarity of the record, how many witnesses do you have for videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miroslav Tadic Defence two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the others -- that are here. So we are trying to see how much time we may need. If you could remember them, these two witnesses, how many hours did you ask for them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you right away. For Mr. Grujicic, Milutin Grujicic, I requested in my motion when I suggested live testimonies, I wanted an examination-in-chief to last between six and seven hours and this is the reason why. Maybe I can reduce that time but what is important, in my view, with Mr. Grujicic is that through him, at least 25 documents will have to be tendered. As far as we are concerned, the examination-in-chief wouldn't last longer than one hour. The second witness is just like we envisaged in the summary. He will go to speak just about an exchange episode or a civilian protection but not more than one hour examination-in-chief; however, for Grujicic, I will do my best. I cannot promise you, but I'm afraid due to the number of documents it will take longer, but not more than six hours, but let's say five to six hours we would require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And I take it that the documents have already been given to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents have been presented to the Prosecution and the documents will be given to the Registry, there is no doubt about that, but we'll do our best to expedite this but these are the documents signed by him and that I have to review with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to make sure that the Prosecution will have already given you what their position is so that we don't waste time during the proceedings asking after each document whether or not they are objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there will be any problems. In the pre-trial procedure, these documents have been given and I will specifically mark these documents and the Prosecutor will be fully informed about all the documents that we intend to tender and they will be able to give their comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well then. Yes, the other counsel, Mr. Pantelic. Videolink witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we already have them on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is one witness and I think -- I'm not maybe able off the top of my head to tell you, around 10 hours, I think, for my witness. He was a member of the Crisis Staff as well as the -- he performed some duties in Odzak so there are documents to introduce through him with regard specifically to Odzak because this is also the area covered by the indictment, but I will be able to -- Your Honour, I will be able to be more precise after the back information from my supporting staff from the field exactly maybe we could also reduce some hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think there will be some exercise to reduce some of the matters which have been sufficiently covered by the evidence. The exhibits have already been given to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, I just collected them during this weekend, last weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I can give them in B/C/S version, it's a couple of the instructions of the Ministry of Defence, in fact, the witness gave me from his personal archive some of these documents and also I will immediately proceed with the official translations. So maybe my learned friends can also, through their interpreters, maybe to speed up things, I mean for their needs but I will do my best with the Registry to -- it's -- I will tell you around five or six pages in total of the documents. There is one telex and the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's all I need to know that the documents will be discussed with the Prosecution. So it's only one witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And maybe this is appropriate opportunity, Your Honour, as I said, I'm not so sure whether I raised that or did I inform the Registry and also Madam Court Officer. The Defence for Blagoje Simic proposed two character witnesses, and finally we have third one which -- the lady should be able to sign her statement during the 18th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And her name is Cvijetic, Desanka a physician by profession. So she will be a third character witness for Blagoje Simic just for the record so that we can arrange that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic, we will have to check how many witnesses actually have already been listed as character witnesses for your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. You granted three witnesses, three character witnesses per each accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I already filed for two character witnesses statement and this is the third one. This is a third one, third character witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What I want clarification on is whether this person you are mentioning today has already been on the list or is it a new witness, you are replacing somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is a new witness, Your Honour, because my first, I would say, proposal for a witness, this gentleman is not able to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you are substituting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So I am substituting instead of Dr. Mesud Nogic I now will ask, respectfully ask to substitute him with Dr. Cvijetic Desanka, also a physician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Pantelic, on this one, let's deal with it tomorrow. We just want to check our lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No problem. I shall also contact Madam Court Officer and we shall try to resolve that matter in direct contact. Also Your Honour, I'm obliged to inform this Trial Chamber in regard to one of the deposition witnesses from Mr. Blagoje Simic Defence. Unfortunately, retired colonel Mr. Vujnovic Gojko was not able to come to testify according to Rule 71. I am now trying to see what was the obstacles. What is his personal situations. Unofficially, I heard that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have already seen your document, your paper which you filed about this and I would rather you find out and then you give correct information to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Tomorrow or next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because I am very shortly, very briefly, unofficially I got the information that a members of Prosecution office contact him, let's say a weeks before and it's not so clear whether he was to somehow prevented to come to testify or what was the -- and I would be very grateful if my learned friend from Prosecution office could check this issue and also from my side, we shall also check with him to see what is the problem with that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can discuss that with the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will discuss to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- outside the sitting hours. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. As for Mr. Zaric Defence, we have just one witness proposed to give his testimony via videolink and this is Witness Mirko Pavic. We already explained in one of our motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you did. I just wanted --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And what I can inform the Trial Chamber is that we don't expect him to testify more than three hours but I have some concerns in respect to this witness because, as we already said to the Trial Chamber, he had a brain stroke and the only actually problem that we have is that he speaks a little bit slower than ordinary people so I cannot make this promise that it would last for three hours or -- we'll just have to wait and see. Mr. Pisarevic did proofing with this witness actually, and he informed me that he has no problem about giving the testimony but he speaks slower than other people so that's the only problem that we have so it might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because I was thinking that if you have such a problem, why don't you get a statement from him and then it can be given to the Prosecution and then they can decide whether or not, like similar to Rule 92 instead of putting him under the strain of being a viva voce witness if he has such a serious health problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We were guided by the decision of the Trial Chamber because we proposed this witness to give testimony by the way of deposition then the ruling came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think at the time we were not aware of his poor health. So you can move him to the 92 witnesses, I think, to save him the problem of being under strain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, having all this in mind, I will contact Mr. Pisarevic as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then yes, because he could still come under videolink if the other problem is travelling. Yeah, please look into that and since your colleague is in the field, he can easily arrange for that. The officials for collecting statements will be going so you can make those arrangements and then he can still come under videolink if the Prosecution wish to have him under cross-examination because I don't want to have a situation where we have videolink and the witness breaks down and then we have to adjourn because the courtroom situation is very critical this is why I'm asking about these witnesses. So I think -- let's switch him to that and then he can come for videolink if cross-examination will be required.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will definitely do what is in the best interest of the witness, not to push him any harder than we need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, and of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly two matters in response to Mr. Pantelic's points. The first is in relation to his scheduled ten-hour Crisis Staff videolink witness. In ten hours one would anticipate the witness will give evidence of many, many facts and I'd certainly ask that we have a proper summary of the facts on which the witness will testify. I don't think we have one yet. The second matter is retired Lieutenant Colonel Vujnovic and Mr. Pantelic's speculation the Prosecution may have spoken to him which I hear about for the first time in Court now. The Prosecution team here puts on the record it has never spoken to Lieutenant Colonel Vujnovic. We will make appropriate inquiries of our colleagues, someone may have spoken to him because of his role on General Talic's command staff, we don't know, but we'll find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour, I agree just for the record of course I never mentioned that my particular learned friends from this team contacted him, maybe that was in another case or I will try to do that to find out and also I hope that my learned friends will help us. With regard to the first issue of course I'll do my best to prepare a summary with the issues that will be discussed so I will fulfill my obligations with regard to that. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the summaries should avoid repetition of the other witness' evidence, the ones we have already heard viva voce. I wanted to find out from the counsel for Mr. Simo Zaric about the statements, Rule 92 statements. I understand they are already ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour. Yes, we have received all the translations. I brought them just this morning and I just couldn't make enough copies for the Trial Chamber. I will be ready to tender them into evidence tomorrow before we start with Mr. Tadic. Also, I have to inform the Trial Chamber that we have collected actually that two 92 bis statements have been certified during our stay in Belgrade and I will have to give these for translation but at this moment, all the statements that we took during our stay in Bosanski Samac in December are ready to be tendered into evidence and it will be done tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think we will find an appropriate moment tomorrow so that tomorrow, the first witness, the accused, should start instead of starting with something else. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So we'll adjourn. Our proceedings will continue tomorrow. I think we are in courtroom 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
